meta.title: mu · Only what's needed.
meta.description: mu is a coding agent with a judgment kernel: a small, fast judge model makes dozens of small decisions in every turn, so the task gets only the context it needs. Command line and desktop app, open source.
meta.og_description: A coding agent that gives the task only the context it needs. Built on pi, with a small, fast judge model for the routine decisions.

ui.footer_credit: mu is built on pi (MIT). Thanks to its authors.

home.lead: mu is a coding agent. A small, fast judge model makes dozens of small decisions for the main model in every turn: what stays in the context, whether a command is safe, whether the work is really done. The main model keeps its attention on the work.
home.cli_hint: Needs Node.js 22.19 or newer. Run mu setup once to connect a model, then mu in a project folder.
home.app_hint: The Windows app isn't signed yet, so SmartScreen shows a warning. Windows on Arm, Linux on Arm and every other download are under Releases.
home.app_alt: The mu desktop app after a bug fix: the conversation in the middle, the Judge tab on the right listing each of the judge's verdicts with its decision point and time, and the kernel bar along the bottom
home.swarm_alt: The Hive tab in the desktop app: three bees investigate one bug at once; the arrows are findings the judge decided were worth delivering
home.board_alt: The plain-language board: what's being done, how far it got and the running account below

chapters.label: When you send a message
paras: Is this a new task, a follow-up or a correction? Should a message that arrives mid-run interrupt now? Does it need skills and tools, or will a one-line answer do?
after: In this turn, the user writes "{prompt}", and in under a second the judge answers: a multi-step task, full effort. Skills and MCP servers the task doesn't need stay out of the context until it does.

chapters.label: When a tool returns
chapters.h2: Output goes through the judge first
paras: A test run or a search can easily return hundreds of lines. The judge decides, chunk by chunk, what matters now; only that enters the context, and the rest is archived behind a pointer, ready when it's needed.
In web pages and MCP results, instructions aimed at the model are withheld before it reads them.

chapters.label: Before acting
chapters.h2: Block what's risky, ask only when it matters
paras: Before a command runs, rules flag anything risky, and the judge checks that you asked for it and that it doesn't cross a constraint you stated. There are three permission modes (Full access, Judge mode and Ask first), and you can switch at any time. In Judge mode, the judge lets through what the task clearly needs and asks you about the rest.

chapters.label: When the turn ends
paras: When the model says it's done, mu checks whether anything verified that, whether the turn drifted and whether to go back to a checkpoint.

/goal <condition> keeps the agent working until the condition holds. The main model checks whether it does, with the judge as the fallback; when the same error comes back again and again, the judge decides whether the approach is a dead end.

chapters.label: The hive
chapters.h2: Several bees at work, the judge in the middle
paras: When several agents work on one hard problem, splitting up the work is easy; communication is hard. Say nothing, and each walks into the same dead end. Say everything, and every context fills with the others' chatter.

In mu's hive, the judge weighs every finding: is it worth sharing, and does it matter to a given bee? Only then does it reach that bee as context. When a later finding overturns an earlier one, the correction goes to every bee that heard it.

chapters.label: The plain-language board
chapters.h2: Working and reporting are different jobs
paras: Models get stronger, and their reports read more and more like notes for a machine. In mu the working model keeps working its own way. Every few tool calls, the judge checks what happened, picks what's really news and hands it to a model chosen for writing plainly, which tells you where things stand.
When a run ends, you see not just "done" but what was actually done.

principles.p: In Judge mode, the judge lets through what the task clearly needs and asks you about the rest.
Each message is judged: small talk, a follow-up or work to do. Skills and MCP servers that aren't needed stay out of the context.
When the context grows, stale tool results are dropped instead of summarized, and summary-free compaction is an option. Before the cache expires, mu judges whether a refresh is worth it.
{points} decision points, each with its own switch and its own judge: the free Jev, mude 1.0 on your Mac or any LLM.

principles.h3: No judge key needed to start
principles.p: Without a judge key, the free Jev on OpenCode Zen answers, and mu says so once a day.
The command line is built on pi, with its models, extensions, skills and session tree. The desktop app runs the same sessions.

home.principles_more: What each of the {points} decision points asks and changes
home.more_h2: One set of accounts, settings and lessons for the command line and the app

more.text: Bring in your Claude Code, Codex and ZCode conversations and carry on in mu.
Sign in with ChatGPT, Grok or Google inside the app; no keys to copy around.
Your corrections and the traps the agent found a way around are kept; a lesson that is recalled and never followed retires itself.
The judge drives it step by step: look at the page, decide once, act; it stops to ask before submitting or paying.
Every verdict and how long it took: /status, mu ledger and the app's Judge tab.
The desktop app speaks English, 简体中文, 繁體中文, 日本語, 한국어 and 8 more.

models.title: Models
models.h1: mude 1.0: a decision model optimized for coding
models.lead: mu's own decision model, trained for the decisions a coding agent makes and state of the art at making them. It runs on your machine, so what it judges never leaves it.
models.mude_h2: A judge that runs on your machine

facts.p: One forward pass answers every question in a decision, each with a probability.
Its server runs on 127.0.0.1. What it judges never leaves your machine.
Both editions are on Hugging Face, free to download.

models.full_p: The full model: bf16, PyTorch, about 4.0 GB. A CUDA GPU is recommended.
models.mac_p: The Mac edition: MLX, 8-bit, a 1.8 GB download. It's the one mu installs.
models.install_intro: One-click install works on Macs with Apple silicon today, with macOS 14 or later and at least 8 GB of memory. On such a Mac, mude is the recommended judge, and mu setup offers it first. While it runs, the server uses about 4 GB.

cli.install: download (resumes after a stop), verify every file, start it on 127.0.0.1, make it the judge
cli.status: what is installed, running and enabled
cli.local_only: mude only: nothing goes to a hosted judge
cli.disable: back to the previous judge; stops its server
cli.uninstall: remove the model and its Python environment

app.text: On a Mac that can run it, the judge step starts with mude selected as the recommended judge, and one click installs it. If an install stops, click Continue installing to pick up where it left off.
The mude card installs, starts and stops it, makes it the judge and uninstalls it. It also has the Local only switch.

models.other_p: Elsewhere, run the full edition (mude-1.0 on Hugging Face) with its own System One server, as its model card shows, and add it to ~/.mu/agent/mu.json as a typesafe judge. MUDE_KEY holds the key the server was started with:
models.other_link: Using mude 1.0 with mu, on its model card

local.p: The judge you used before stays on as mude's fallback. It answers what mude can't (when mude's server isn't running or mude is unsure) and always handles the two injection screens: tool descriptions and tool output. When that judge is hosted, what goes to it leaves your machine.
mude is the only judge, and nothing goes to a hosted judge. When mude can't answer, the decision point does what it would do without a judge.

mubench.title: mubench 1.0
mubench.h1: mubench 1.0: decision models, scored on a coding agent's decisions
mubench.lead: On mubench's main board, every item is a request mu sent to a decision model, word for word, in a real coding session on an open-source repository. Each answer is scored by the cost of its consequences, and every model is compared with mu running without a decision model.
mubench.main_intro: {items} requests from {tasks} coding tasks on open-source repositories.
mubench.few_short: Few items or an unstable score
mubench.note_few: Few items or an unstable score: fewer than {items} items, items from fewer than {tasks} tasks, or mu already right more than {baseline}% of the time with no decision model.
mubench.score_note: Without a decision model, mu's mistakes have a cost. A score is how much of that cost a model removes: 100 removes all of it, 0 is no better, below 0 is worse. It isn't accuracy; that's in decision accuracy below.
mubench.note_threat_acc: Malicious-instruction detection isn't shown here either: none of the main board's 19 such requests contains an attack, and every model, as well as mu with no decision model, gets them all right. The sub-board has none yet.

method.p: Summed over the capability's decision points: f is the average cost per check with no decision model, r the same with the model, and w the decision point's weight (3 for safety gates, 2 for decisions made every turn, 1 for the rest). 100 means all of that cost is removed, 0 no better than no decision model, below 0 worse.

mubench's pooled score over every decision point. It equals the mean of the capability scores, each weighted by its share of the cost with no decision model (the "Weight in overall" row); the costs and weights were fixed before any model was scored. Not equal weights: item counts differ about 60-fold between capabilities, and equal weights would let the smallest, noisiest ones swing the result.

The thin lines on the overall charts. A bootstrap with 1,000 draws, resampled within each decision point: by task on the main board, since requests from one session aren't independent, and by scenario on the sub-board.
The capability has no items, or mu loses nothing there without a decision model, so the score is undefined.

mubench.sub_intro: {items} scenarios written for mubench and scored the same way. Their mix of decisions differs from real sessions, so the two boards are scored separately and never added together.
mubench.acc_intro: The share of checks a model gets right (an item can have several checks), with mu running without a decision model as the first row. Here every check counts the same, whatever its mistakes cost, so accuracy and score can rank models differently.
mubench.chart_acc_alt: Bar chart of decision accuracy, with 95% intervals. Main board: {main}. Sub-board: {sub}.
mubench.chart_overall_alt: Bar chart of the main board's overall scores, with 95% intervals: {list}. No decision model: 0.
mubench.chart_sub_alt: Bar chart of the sub-board's overall scores, with 95% intervals: {list}. No decision model: 0.
mubench.chart_caps_alt: Bar charts of the eight capability scores on the main board; the numbers are in the table above.
mubench.chart_scoring_alt: How mubench scores a decision model: a real request mu sent to a decision model in a coding session; the decision the model under test makes; the cost of its consequences; that cost compared with mu running without a decision model.

caps_text.permission: Whether an action may go ahead: is a flagged command what the user asked for, can a call be approved for the user, does it break a constraint the user set.
caps_text.threat: Whether outside content, such as a web page, a search result or an MCP reply, carries instructions aimed at the AI, and whether an MCP tool's description slips in commands that have nothing to do with the tool.
caps_text.compression: When the context is nearly full, which old tool output to keep; whether an old result is still worth its tokens; which parts of a tool's output can stay out of the context.
caps_text.loading: Which packs and skills a task needs; whether and when to tell the model about diagnostics or outside events; whether to keep the prompt cache warm.
caps_text.routing: What kind of message this is and how much effort it deserves; whether a mid-run message changes course now or waits; also review triage, finding files and the browser's next step.
caps_text.progress: Whether the turn is done, whether the agent should keep going, whether the goal is met, whether the work has drifted or should be rewound, and whether output breaks a rule.
caps_text.memory: What is worth remembering, whether it is already known, which lesson applies now, whether the agent followed it, and whether it can become a skill.
caps_text.multiagent: What to pass between agents in a hive, to whom, and how it relates to earlier findings; whether a subagent's changes stay in scope; which role and thinking level a subtask gets.

enterprise.title: Enterprise
enterprise.h1: Need a decision model customized for you and your company?
enterprise.lead: In every turn, mu asks a decision model dozens of small questions: may this command run, which old output is worth keeping, is the work done. We can tune one to how your team answers them, run it on your own machines, and show you in numbers what it changes.
enterprise.mude_h2: Start from mude 1.0, on your own machines

run.p: One click in the desktop app, or one command: mu judge mude install. mu downloads the 8-bit MLX edition, checks every file, starts it on 127.0.0.1 and makes it the judge.
The full bf16 model, with its own System One server. A CUDA GPU is recommended. mu reaches it as a judge over your own network.

enterprise.mude_link: More about mude 1.0 on the Models page
enterprise.custom_h2: Tuned to how your team decides

steps.p: We start from the decisions that matter to you: what counts as risky in your codebase, what your review policy asks for, how work should be routed.
We score your current setup on those decisions the way mubench does: each answer by the cost of its consequences.
We fine-tune a decision model on your decision points, workflows and rules.
The same scoring again, next to your current setup, so you can see what changed before you switch.

enterprise.mu_h2: Works with mu out of the box

mu.b: The judge in the CLI and the app
mu.text: mu judge mude install on the command line, or the mude card in the desktop app's Settings → Judges.
With mu judge mude enable --local-only, mude is the only judge and nothing goes to a hosted judge. When mude can't answer, the decision point does what it would do without a judge.
Decision points in shadow mode still ask and record their verdicts, but change nothing, so you can watch a model before you trust it.
Every verdict is recorded on your machine: the answers and their probabilities, how long it took, and whether the judge or a fallback gave it. Read it with mu ledger or in the app's Judge tab.

faq.q: Can we try mude 1.0 before we talk?
faq.a: Yes. It's free under the MIT license. Install it, put your decision points in shadow mode, and read its verdicts in the ledger.
No. A decision model only answers mu's decisions. Your coding model, and where it runs, stay your choice.
Nothing mude answers: it runs on your machines. With Local only on, nothing goes to a hosted judge either. Your coding model is separate, and what it sees goes wherever it runs.

faq.q: How would we know a custom model is better?
faq.a: We score it the way mubench does, on your own decision points, before and after, next to your current setup. You see the numbers before you switch.
